entry.title: exoALMA: A search for the youngest exoplanets

link.title: exoALMA: A search for the youngest exoplanets

entry.content:
The Goals

The program has had three main objectives: 1) to search for embedded protoplanets by examining the substructures that they create in the disk’s structure and gas kinematics, 2) to constrain the physical properties of these disk, such as their velocity, temperature, and density structure, and 3) to identify large-scale signatures of instabilities, such as GI, VSI or MRI.

Over the past decade, disk observations of the dust continuum at millimeter and NIR wavelengths at sufficiently high-angular resolution have shown that planet-forming disks are highly structured, exhibiting symmetric gaps and rings, asymmetric crescents and arcs, or spirals (Bae et al., 2023; Benisty et al., 2023). The dust distribution reflects the underlying gas dynamics, as it depends on the strength of the coupling of grains to the gas motion (St-number). So, are most dust continuum rings formed via the accumulation of pebbles in gas pressure bumps? Is this process the primary mechanism driving the formation of dust substructure? Alternative processes include ice-lines (e.g., Saito and Sirono, 2011; Zhang et al., 2015), dust coagulation fronts (e.g., Ohashi et al., 2021), or second-generation dust rings via planetesimal collisions (e.g., Jiang and Ormel, 2021; Testi et al., 2022). To further examine the processes shaping the widely observed multi-wavelength dust substructures, analyzing the gas kinematics of protoplanetary disks is the next essential step.

After the exciting discoveries and the potential of early gas kinematical studies of protoplanetary disks, the first ALMA Large Program focusing on the analysis of gas kinematics around planet-forming disks was accepted and observed in ALMA’s cycle 8 2021/2022 (ID: 2021.1.01123.L, PI: R. Teague). The exoALMA campaign targeted 15 large and bright planet-forming disks, most of which transition disks, at unprecedented spectral (~28 m s−1) and angular resolution (~0.1″) (Loomis et al., 2025; Teague et al., 2025), pushing ALMA’s capabilities to its current limit. The observational setup targeted the disk continuum and the molecular lines 12CO (J = 3−2), 13CO (J = 3−2), and CS (J = 7−6) in ALMA Band 7 with ~10 h on source-integration time, making it some of the deepest disk observations to date.

As the program’s name suggests, its primary goal was to search for the youngest still embedded exoplanets, via the distinct imprints they leave on the gas velocity structure of the disk. However, with these exquisite observations, it has also been possible to investigate the dynamic and physical structure of protoplanetary disks in great detail. Planet formation is not an isolated process, but presumably happens simultaneously with (magneto)hydrodynamical instabilities that affect the disk’s evolution (Lesur et al., 2023). It is thus crucial to investigate these processes to obtain a comprehensive picture of the physical and dynamical structure of planet-forming disks, for which exoALMA provided the necessary data quality.

In summary, the program has had three main objectives: 1) to search for embedded protoplanets by examining the substructures that they create in the disk’s structure and gas kinematics, 2) to constrain the physical properties of these disk, such as their velocity, temperature, and density structure, and 3) to identify large-scale signatures of instabilities, such as GI, VSI or MRI. In the following paragraphs, I will summarize the main findings from the first wave of 17 exoALMA papers, on all of which I am a co-author, concerning these objectives.

Summary of exoALMA results

The gallery of the exoALMA disk sample with its 12CO (3-2) peak intensity and 0.9 mm dust continuum maps are presented in the two figures below. Teague et al., 2025 provides a detailed overview of the project’s design, scientific goals, and key findings. It is already essential to note that the exoALMA sample is biased towards the largest and brightest planet-forming disks, allowing for the observation of their molecular line emission at high resolution. Furthermore, these disks were chosen to have already well-characterized dust substructures, indicative of the embedded planets we aimed to detect.

Figure 1: Gallery of the exoALMA sample, 12CO (3-2) peak intensity maps, with variable field of view but same synthesized beam sizes of 0.15″ denoted in the lower left corner. From Teague et al., 2025.

Optimized methodology

First, I summarize the optimized methods we developed within the collaboration to handle the exoALMA dataset. To begin, the ALMA interferometric observations must be calibrated and imaged to produce continuum and molecular line data cubes for analysis. Loomis et al., 2025 presents these methodologies, which were specifically developed for the data quality of exoALMA. We paid particular attention to the alignment of different execution blocks and phase decoherence, to not introduce artificial features resembling kinematic deviations we aim to detect. The robustness of the observed non-Keplerian features was further ensured by an alternative technique from CLEAN employing regularized maximum likelihood imaging, which allows for super-resolution images (Zawadzki et al., 2025). We benchmarked the most widely used hydrodynamics and radiative transfer codes, demonstrating high agreement when forward-modeling and interpreting kinematic perturbations of modeled planet-disk interactions (Bae et al., 2025).

In Izquierdo et al., 2025, we present an improved methodology to account for the complex gaseous structures of our targets through channel-map modeling of the molecular line emissions. Utilizing and further developing the discminer code-package (Izquierdo et al., 2021), we could accurately describe the disks’ emission morphologies and identify variations in the properties of these lines across our sample. We paid particular focus to the exact extraction of line properties, developing a novel two-component fit to disentangle the front and back side emission in our line moment maps. To evaluate the robustness of our moment maps, which form the basis of most of the analysis, Hilder et al., 2025 investigated the spatial correlations derived from our model’s posterior distribution. Our findings indicated that parameter uncertainties are underestimated by an order of magnitude when applying a more realistic probabilistic noise model.

Physical properties

The second cluster of papers focuses on determining the disk’s physical properties, both on a global and more localized scale, i.e., radial profiles. Also in Izquierdo et al., 2025, we present the discminer best-fit parameters of the exoALMA disks, including Keplerian stellar masses, geometrical properties, and gas surface emission heights. While in the discminer framework, the latter is described via an exponentially tapered power-law, Galloway-Sprietsma et al., 2025 investigated substructures in the emission heights and line intensities. The paper further presents the global 2D temperature structures of a subsample of disks and finds a positive correlation between the emission height, disk extents, and gas disk masses.

The measurement of gas disk masses and surface densities from observations is of central importance, as it influences the overall disk evolution and comprises the available mass budget for forming planets in disks. Several works in our collaboration have hence focused on its determination. Rosotti et al., 2025 presents a model for the aforementioned correlation between emission heights and gas surface densities (Galloway-Sprietsma et al., 2025; Paneque-Carreño et al., 2025), finding a median CO depletion of factor ~ 20 with respect to the interstellar medium. Yoshida et al., 2025 was able to measure the gas surface density from pressure-broadened CO line wings in the face-on transition disk of RXJ1604.3-2130A (see also J1604). Another exciting aspect of the exoALMA dataset was the determination of gas surface density through modeling the gas rotation curve (Lodato et al., 2023; Martire et al., 2024; Veronesi et al., 2021). This technique offers a significant advantage, as it does not require conversion factors to relate the measured CO line emission to H2 abundances. Therefore, it is considered a more reliable estimate of the true gas disk masses.

Fitting to the rotation curves provided through my work (Stadler et al., 2025), Longarini et al., 2025a obtained dynamical gas disk mass estimates for 10 sources of the exoALMA sample, all of which appear gravitationally stable (Qtoom > 1). In addition, we combined the dynamical disk masses with the disk mass estimated from optical thin dust continuum emission. We found an averaged dust-to-gas mass ratio of ~ 400, statistically in line with the standard value of 100. Finally, using ancillary N2H+ (J = 3−2) observations, Trapman et al., 2025 measured disk masses based on integrated line fluxes and thermochemical models for 19 disks. These emission-based gas masses agree well with the kinematically measured ones within a factor of three, although they are systematically lower than dynamical estimates by a factor of two.

Substructures in emission and kinematics

The last set of papers investigates and interprets the observed emission and kinematical substructures in the search for embedded protoplanets and signatures of large-scale instabilities. Curone et al., 2025 presents the 0.9 mm dust continuum maps of our sample (see below figure), modeling and analyzing their substructures, asymmetries, and faint outer disk emission. The paper also provides the best-fit geometrical parameters of the continuum visibility fits. Most asymmetric continuum disks with inner dust cavities show higher mass accretion rates and NIR excess, suggesting a connection between outer disk dust substructures and inner disk properties. Galloway-Sprietsma et al., 2025 further reports the presence of substructures in the emission surfaces and radial intensity profiles in nearly all of the disks. Within each disk, these substructures often align between molecular tracers, intensity profiles, and kinematic perturbations.

Figure 2: Gallery of the exoALMA sample, dust continuum maps at 0.9 mm on same scales (1.2″×1.2″) with varying beam sizes and scale bar in the lower left and right corner, respectively, adapted from Curone et al., 2025. Note that the scale bar of 30 au corresponds to the size of the Solar System (semi-major axis of Neptune) for comparison.

Investigating the exoALMA channel maps in the search for localized kinematic substructures has probably been one of the most anticipated papers of the collaboration. Pinte et al., 2025 highlights these velocity kinks, spiral arms, and filament-like features observed. We uncover the signatures of embedded planets in five disks (AA Tau, J1615, J1842, LkCa15 & SY Cha), with modeled masses ranging from 1 to 5 MJup at orbital distances between 80-330 au. In the study of non-planetary driven features, Barraza-Alfaro et al., 2025 investigates large-scale turbulence within the disks observed by exoALMA. While the vertical shear instability (VSI) was not detected, some of the spiral-like velocity patterns observed could potentially be explained by the magneto-rotational instability (MRI) or gravitational instability (GI), although most of our disks have been determined to have gravitationally stable disk masses. On the other hand, some of the smooth, dynamically non-perturbed disks appear almost laminar. Finally, in exoALMA XVII., Wölfer et al., 2025 characterized the gas kinematics around dust asymmetries in the sample. The paper qualitatively compares the observed features to analytical vortex models and hydrodynamic simulations of the Rossby Wave instability (RWI) and dead zones. While the observations cannot provide evidence for the presence of an anticyclonic vortex for most disks, the disk around HD 135344B shows the most resemblance.

Conclusions and what comes next

To be written. Link to another story with link text.

The program

Teague et al. (2025): exoALMA. I. Science Goals, Project Design, and Data Products, The Astrophysical Journal Letters 984, L6 · arXiv · DOI

Personal context

This was the main project of my PhD. This summary story was taken from the second chapter of my PhD thesis.

entry.title: J1604: A kinematically detected planet candidate

link.title: J1604: A kinematically detected planet candidate

entry.content:
The question

What is the physical origin of the cavity in the transition disk of J1604? How do the shadows cast by its inner misaligned disk affect its dust and gas millimeter emission?

General Context

Transition disks are protoplanetary disks with inner dust continuum cavities. There are several physical mechanisms that can create these cavities, including gas photoevaporation, magneto-hydrodynamic instabilities, or clearing by massive companions. Observing these disks at high angular and spectral resolution with ALMA is ideal for mapping their gas velocity structure and probing companion–disk interactions.

Method

In this work, we present ALMA Band 6 dust and gas observations of the transition disk around RXJ1604.3–2130 A, known to feature nearly symmetric shadows in scattered light, and aim to search for non-Keplerian velocity features. We studied the 12CO line channel maps and moment maps of the line-of-sight velocity and peak intensity. We fitted a Keplerian model of the channel-by-channel emission to study line profile differences and produced deprojected radial profiles for all velocity components.

Figure 1: J1604 overview. (a) SPHERE infrared observations show a ring and a highly depleted cavity in small grains. The two shadows indicate a misaligned inner disk, that is unresolved and hidden by a coronagraph. (b) ALMA dust continuum observations show the same features. (c) ALMA 12CO velocity residual map after subtraction of a Keplerian model show a major residual (in red) right within the mm ring (reported in black contours). The white cross indicates the location of the planet candidate. Credit: Stadler et al. (2023).

What we found

Azimuthal brightness variations in the 12CO line and dust continuum are broadly aligned with the shadows detected in scattered-light observations. We find a strong localized non-Keplerian feature toward the west within the continuum ring, which accounts for $\Delta v_\phi/v_\mathrm{kep} \sim0.4$ or $\Delta v_z/v_\mathrm{kep}\sim0.04$, depending on whether the perturbation is in the rotational or vertical direction. A tightly wound spiral is also detected and extends over 300 degrees in azimuth, possibly connected to the localized non-Keplerian feature. Finally, a bending of the iso-velocity contours within the gas cavity indicates a highly perturbed inner region, possibly related to the presence of a warp connecting to the misaligned inner disk.

Conclusions and what comes next

While broadly aligned with the scattered-light shadows, the localized non-Keplerian feature cannot be solely due to changes in temperature. Instead, we interpret the kinematic feature as tracing a massive companion located at the edge of the dust continuum ring. We speculate that the spiral is caused by buoyancy resonances driven by planet–disk interactions. However, this potential planet at 41 au cannot explain the gas-depleted cavity, the low accretion rate, and the misaligned inner disk, which suggests the presence of another companion closer in. This transition disk has also been part of the exoALMA disk sample.

The paper

Stadler, Benisty, Izquierdo et al. (2023): A kinematically detected planet candidate in a transition disk, Astronomy & Astrophysics 670, L1 · arXiv · DOI

Personal context

My research on the transition disk J1604 was the first project of my PhD and also my first collaboration with Andrés Izquierdo. During a summer research visit to ESO Garching in August 2022, he taught me how to apply his Discminer code to the dataset that ultimately led to the detection of this planet candidate and the publication of a Letter in A&A.

entry.title: The bumpy road to planet formation

link.title: The bumpy road to planet formation

entry.content:
The question

How do dynamically evolving gas pressure bumps affect the observational properties of protoplanetary disks? Can we observationally distinguish between planetary versus zonal flow origin of pressure bumps?

General Context

Over the last years, large (sub-)millimeter surveys of protoplanetary disks in different star-forming regions have well constrained the demographics of disks, such as their millimeter luminosities, spectral indices, and disk radii. Additionally, several high-resolution observations have revealed an abundance of substructures in the disk’s dust continuum. The most prominent are ring-like structures, which are likely caused by pressure bumps trapping dust particles. Still, the origins and characteristics of these pressure bumps need to be understood in more detail.

Method

We perform one-dimensional gas and dust evolution simulations, setting up models with varying gas pressure bump features, including their amplitude and location, growth time, and number of bumps. We subsequently run radiative transfer calculations to obtain synthetic images, from which we obtain the different quantities of observations.

Figure 1: Synthetic ALMA dust continuum images of various bump models. Credit: Stadler et al. (2022).

What we found

The outermost pressure bump determines the disk’s dust size across different millimeter wavelengths and the observed dust masses of disks with optically thick inner bumps (<40 au) are underestimated by up to an order of magnitude. Our modeled dust traps need to form early (a few ten-thousand years), fast (on gas viscous timescales), and must be long-lived (a few million years) to be consistent with the observations of high millimeter luminosities and low spectral indices of disks. While the planetary bump models can reproduce these observables irrespective of the opacity prescription, the highest opacities are needed for the dynamic bump model, which mimics zonal flows in disks, to be in line with observations.

Conclusions and what comes next

Our findings favor the planetary over the zonal flow origin of pressure bumps and support the idea that planet formation should already occur in early Class 0/I stages of circumstellar disks (after a few ten- to hundred thousand years). The determination of the disk’s effective size through its outermost pressure bump also delivers a possible answer to why disks in recent low-resolution surveys appear to have the same sizes across different millimeter wavelengths. The study of disk gas kinematics via molecular line observations with ALMA can help to constrain the properties of these gas pressure bumps (see exoALMA VI).

The paper

Stadler, Gárate, Pinilla et al. (2022): The impact of dynamic pressure bumps on the observational properties of protoplanetary disks, Astronomy & Astrophysics 668, A104 · arXiv · DOI

Personal context

This publication originated from my Masters thesis at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy (MPIA) in Heidelberg within the The genesis of planets research group of Prof. Paola Pinilla and under co-supervision of Dr. Matthias Gárate.
entry.summary: How pressure bumps change what we observe in protoplanetary disks
